action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Pillar II capital add-on for banks with excessive trading activities. Two separate threshold indicators, a volume-based indicator and a risk-based indicator, will be used to determine whether a bank must face a surcharge. If the bank exceeds either of the indicators, a surcharge will be imposed. The volume-based indicator consists of all non-derivative assets in the held-for-trading (HFT) assets category, all short positions in the HFT liabilities category, and all derivatives in the HFT category which are not used for hedging of the banks’ own positions in their banking books. (It will be assumed that 20% of the derivatives in the HFT category are used for hedging, unless banks can demonstrate that the proportion is higher than 20%.) A capital surcharge will be applied if the volume-based indicator exceeds 15% of the bank’s total assets, and the surcharge will equal the amount by which the volume indicator exceeds the threshold. The risk-based indicator consists of the regulatory capital requirements for market risk, excluding the market risk capital requirements for foreign exchange risk. A capital surcharge will be applied if this “adjusted” market risk capital requirement exceeds 10% of total regulatory capital requirements, and the surcharge will equal three times the amount by which market risk capital requirements exceed the threshold.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In 2009, banks were recommended to retain profits starting for 2008 and 2009. The conditions under which profits shoudl be retained have been revised in following years. In general, the measure has a countercyclical nature and targets the improvement of bank’s capital resilience (decrease the systemic risk by raising banks’ loss-absorbing capacity and thus reducing the probability of individual default). It was implemented, and renewed,  via orders by the Deputy-governor responsible for Banking Supervision Department. The measure concerns all credit institution. Profit distribution restrictions are communicated to the banks at the beginning of the year, following the reference year for which the profit distribution restrictions apply. Following 2011, banks were recommended not to distribute a dividend for 2011, unless they meet at least one of the following conditions: (i) Total capital ratio should be higher than 15%; (ii) Tier-one capital adequacy should be higher than 13%; (iii) The complex CAMELOS rating assigned by Banking Supervision Department of BNB for the bank's activities in 2011 should be not less than 2; (iv) For subsidiary of credit institutions, the Tier-one capital of the parent bank should be higher than 9%, i.e. the parent bank should not be subject to recapitalization as recommended by the European Banking Authority in December 2011. Following 2012, banks recommended not to distribute a dividend for 2012, unless they meet at least one of the following conditions:  (i) Total capital ratio should be higher than 14%; (ii) Tier-one capital adequacy should be higher than 12%; (iii) The ratio, which measures the coverage of the deposits from institutions, individuals and households with liquid assets, should be not less than 25%.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
Keeping the guidelines for calculating and the requirements for the minimum level of the ratio of the amount of assets to the net cash flow by maturity time bands (7, 30, 90 and 180 days) unchanged, in 2010 several new provisions were introduced to BNB Ordinance No.11 on Bank Liquidity Management and Supervision, and existing qualitative provisions were supplemented in order to strengthen the liquidity risk management in banks. The amendments were related to harmonization of qualitative requirements to bank liquidity management with the EU framework. As an element of liquidity and liquidity risk management, banks were required to maintain liquidity buffers to help them overcome liquidity problems in an adverse environment. The new provisions enhanced the use of stress tests. The results thereof would be used by banks as a basis for determining the amount and composition of their liquidity buffers and positions, and for updating their contingency action plans and ‘liquid crisis’ scenarios.
Those amendments resulted in a more conservative treatment of the respective risks, thus providing the conditions for their better management within individual banks.

The amendments to BNB Ordinance No. 7 on Large Exposures of Banks provide for changes in the regime of treatment of large interbank exposures. The scope of permitted ways used by banks to reduce their large exposures is reduced. An exemption from the regime will be granted only for specific types of receivables, characterized by high liquidity and low credit risk. In this relation, the amendments impose a requirement for partial inclusion in the large exposure treatment regime of exposures to parent banks and subsidiary banks from a group. The purpose is to provide additional protection against excessive concentration of exposures to companies belonging to the same group. The amendments provide additional clarifications as to the recognition of the effect of using credit protection instruments.

This change was introduced due to a higher than projected increase in bank household and corporate placements, coupled by a decrease in the off-balance sheet items. description: A credit institution may conclude a legal arrangement with a person in a special relationship only if such an arrangement is concluded under terms and conditions not more favourable than the credit institution's common terms and conditions.  The credit institution's exposure to such person exceeding HRK 50 000 may be incurred or increased only by a unanimous decision of all management board members and subject to prior approval of the supervisory board. According to the Credit Institutions Act (2014) persons in a special relationship with a credit institution are: (1) the credit institution's shareholders owning 5% or more of shares with voting rights at the credit institution's general meeting; (2) the members of the credit institution's management and supervisory board and its procurators; (3) persons who have concluded employment contracts with the credit institution the provisions of which imply that these persons have a significant influence over the operation of the credit institution or the contracts in which the remuneration for the work of these persons is determined in accordance with the special criteria, different from those applied to the persons who have concluded the standard employment contracts, where these persons are not referred to in item (1) or (2) of this paragraph; (4) legal persons in which the credit institution holds a participation or in which members of the credit institution's management board, supervisory board or its procurators hold a participation; (5) legal persons whose members of the management or supervisory body or procurators are at the same time members of the credit institution's management or supervisory board or its procurators; (6) legal persons whose member of the management board owns 10% or more of shares with voting rights at the credit institution's general meeting; (7) the members of the management board, supervisory board or procurators of the undertaking which is, directly or indirectly, the credit institution's parent undertaking or the credit institution's subsidiary; (8) third persons acting for the account of persons referred to in items (1) to (7) of this paragraph in relation to the activities which would incur or increase the credit institution's exposure. (2) Persons in a special relationship with a credit institution shall also be the following: (1) persons connected with the persons referred to in paragraph (1), items (1) to (7) of this Article in the manner referred to in Article 3, item (18) of this Act; and (2) immediate family members of natural persons referred to in paragraph (1), items (1) to (7) of this Article.

subcategory: Liquidity ratios and deposit coverage ratios
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
Banks are required to maintain a minimum liquid assets ratio (stock liquidity ratio) of 20%, being the ratio of “liquid” assets to the liabilities  as defined per Central Bank of Cyprus directives. The liquidity ratio is calculated for items which are denominated in euro. Applies to banks with local operations.       
The liabilities included in the calculation of the liquid assets ratio comprise:  (i) Total customer deposits, irrespective of maturity; (ii) All liabilities which do not fall under the definition of point (i) above and are payable within the next 12 months. Included in the said liabilities are commitments and contingencies which are expected to result in outflows within the next 12 months, as recognised and reported in the various time bands; (iii) In the case of commitments that relate to unutilised credit lines to connected persons (banks and non-banks) or to other banks, the respective amounts shall not be included within liabilities, but instead they shall be deducted from the liquid assets on the basis of the following percentages: 
1. for credit lines to connected persons (banks and non-banks) – 100% 
2. for credit lines to other banks – 50%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
Clients with negative net wealth (debt exceeds assets)   should pay off new mortgages with an installment at least corresponding to the installment of a mortgage loan with a fixed rate of interest (not lower than 4 pct.) and an amortization profile of 30 years. 

If the client chooses an interest only loan or a loan with a variable rate of interest, the  entire difference up to a corresponding installment of a fixed rate loan should be used to amortise the  housing loan.

The guidelines refer to lending standards in areas with significant real estate price increases: København, Frederiksberg, Dragør, Tårnby, Albertslund, Ballerup, Brøndby, Gentofte, Gladsaxe, Glostrup, Herlev, Hvidovre, Høje-Taastrup, Ishøj, Lyngby-Taarbæk, Rødovre, Vallensbæk og Aarhus.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Levy on credit institutions (balance sheet items), with proceeds accruing to a bank resolution fund. The tax base are total liabilities minus liabilities to customers, profit participation right capital, funds for general banking risks, equity (core Tier 1 capital) funds for general banking risks. The levy was introduced through the Restructuring Act of December 2010 and the Restructuring Fund Ordinance of July 2011. The levy is determined on the basis of the approved annual statements for the last business year ending prior to March 1 of the relevant contribution year. Tax base is determined on an entity not a group level. The tax is payable on 30 September of each year. First payment was made on 30 September 2011. Some additional points to note: (i) There is a cap of 20% of annual net income. (ii) There is a minimum charge of 5% (therefore this is payable even if the bank has losses). In 2011 the levy raised € 600 million and not the predicted €1.3 billion.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
The Law 3869/2010 for heavily indebted households enables individuals to pay their overdue debts in small instalments by restructuring existing debt obligations. According to the provisions of Law, the procedure has three steps: out-of-court settlement, in – court compromise and judicial settlement. The Law prohibits the restructuring of recent debt obligations which have been undertaken by the borrower over the last year before submitting the application for debt restructuring. In addition, the restructuring of debt obligations to the State, Municipalities and Public Organizations is also prohibited. Borrowers who wish to benefit from the provisions of Law should provide accurate information for their financial situation and assets, so as strategic defaulters to be deterred. 
During the whole process and until the issuance of the final Court Decision, execution measures are suspended and especially for mortgage payments, the Court may issue an interim decision to determine the monthly installments, based on the financial situation of the borrower. After the submission of the petition for debt restructuring, claims which are not covered by collateral cease to bear interest while claims backed by collateral will bear interest equal to the one imposed on non-delinquent debts, until the issuance of the final Court decision. 
The final Court decision may rule the liquidation of borrower’s assets and if the estimated value is not adequate to cover the outstanding amount then the Court will determine monthly installment for a period of four years, covering the sum of debt obligations, which will be proportionally distributed to the creditors. The imposed installment for debt service will be based on the financial situation of the borrower taking into account his family needs. However, if the borrower delays any installment for more than three months or is frequently in delay, the Court may declare his forfeiture from the settlement, after creditors’ such request.
The Law also foresees the possibility of debt write -offs for borrowers who are completely unable to repay their loans, due to chronic unemployment or very serious health problems. 
Protection of the main residence: The Court may decide to appoint a liquidator in order to proceed with the liquidation process of the borrower’s assets. In such a case, secured creditors are satisfied in priority from the product of liquidation while unsecured creditors rank after them. The Law provides protection for the main residence of the debtor to be exempted from the liquidation process, provided that the main residence does not exceed the size set by the tax laws for the acquisition of first residence, plus a premium of 50%.  In such a case, the Court restructures the debt obligations of the borrower so as to repay a total amount up to 85% of the objective value of the property. A grace period may be granted to the borrower; however, the duration of the settlement cannot exceed a period of 20 years. The payable interest rate cannot exceed the one that is currently applicable to the performing loans or the average variable interest rate for residential loans, using as a reference rate the interest rate on the main refinancing operations (MRO) of ECB. If the borrower fails to meet the repayment schedule for at least four monthly installments, then creditors can proceed even to the liquidation of the main residence.

description:

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
This Law provides the opportunity to borrowers with performing exposures, under certain prerequisites, to pay their debts under a facilitation programme with favorable conditions. The program concerns loan agreements which were initially signed before the 30.06.2010, even if there are subsequent amendments or renewals of the original contracts. Borrowers could be workers in the public or private sector, unemployed or pensioners. 
The preconditions for joining the programme are the following:  the main residence of the borrower has been given as collateral, the tax value of the said property should not exceed €180.000 (€200.000 for families with three or more children), the tax value of the entire real estate property of the borrower should not exceed €250.000 (€300.000 for families with three or more children), the whole value of deposits and securities of the borrower should not exceed €10.000 (€15.000 for families with three or more children), the total outstanding capital balance should not exceed €150.000, the taxable income should not exceed €15.000  for single persons and €25.000 for married couples (increased by €5.000 for families with three or more children, disabled persons or families with disabled persons) and workers whose taxable income has decreased at least 20% compared with the taxable income of 2009. 
The facilitation programme provides a grace period of 48 months. During the grace period, the monthly installment is limited up to the 30% of the monthly family income; the remaining amount of the initial monthly installment is capitalized and should be repaid at the end of the facilitation programme. 
In the case of borrowers with even lower incomes (up to the limit of €9.000 for single persons, €15.000 for married couples, €13.000 for disabled singles or €20.000 for married couples with three or more children or families with disabled persons) the monthly installment should be computed with an interest rate equal to the interest rate of the ECB main refinancing operations (MRO) plus a premium of 0.75%, only if a higher interest rate is defined at the original contract. Like above, the remaining amount of the initial monthly installment is capitalized and should be repaid at the end of the facilitation programme. 
Especially for unemployed benefited with the unemployment allowance or no income at all, a special 6 months period is provided during the grace period where the borrower is facilitated with zero amount installments. Again, the amount of the initial monthly installment is capitalized and should be repaid at the end of the facilitation programme. 
The new monthly installment should be proportionally distributed to the creditors. A borrower is obligated to inform creditors of any change in his income or assets within one month.

description:
The special liquidator role could be assigned to a legal person (previously reserved only to physical persons) and in addition the same physical or legal person may be appointed liquidator to multiple special liquidations, thus enabling the operating consolidation of multiple special liquidations. Moreover, the Special Liquidation Committee (SLC) is established and has been given the task of consenting, or not, to special liquidators applications for the liquidation of assets and the restructuring of loans.  
The special liquidator has the right to sign reconciliations with borrowers, whose total loan obligations are limited to € 20.000; however, the SLC is required to consent for loan obligations of higher value. The reconciliations concern the partial debt forgiveness of loan principals. 
The special liquidator shall decide for the restructuring of exposures, both performing and non-performing, subject to the aggregate limit of € 250.000 for each borrower. For the restructuring of loan portfolios of higher value, the approval of SLC is required. The restructuring measures may concern the extension of loan repayment period or reduction of loan interest rates. 
In addition, the special liquidator shall decide for the auction of real estate properties, which are owned by credit institutions under liquidation or are pledged as collateral from borrowers, if the tax value of the property is less than € 150.000 and the first strike price exceeds the 7/10ths of the accounting value. In any other case the approval of the SLC is required. 
In the same vein, the auction of loans, equities, bonds, corporate shares and other holdings are subject to the same limits, meaning the special liquidator may decide for accounting values less than € 150.000 and if the first strike price exceeds the 7/10ths of the accounting value or if the securities are listed on a regulated market. In all other cases, the approval of SLC is required. 
The unanimous decision of SLC is required for loan reconciliations and restructurings and auctions of assets valued more than € 1.000.000

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Government Council for Private Debt Management is established and will be composed by the Ministers of Finance, Development and Competitiveness, Justice and Labor. The Council is mandated to promote the necessary actions for the more efficient resolution of non-performing debt of households, corporations and legal entities. More specifically, the Council is responsible for the establishment of a permanent debt resolution mechanism, the modification of the existing legal framework, the improvement of the institutional framework for the real estate market and the provision of public information and counseling services. The Council will determine the amount of “reasonable leaving expenses” based on official statistical data, on a yearly basis, which will be taken into account during the out-of-court workout and judicial process. In addition, the Council will set the prerequisites for borrowers to be classified as “cooperative borrowers” and these prerequisites will be incorporated in the Bank of Greece’s Code of Conduct.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The Bank of Greece, with the objective of accelerating the efforts of banks to address the issue of non-performing exposures, introduces a comprehensive framework of NPEs management, portfolio segmentation, modification of loan terms on a case-by-case basis and resolution options. Moreover, it establishes a detailed NPEs monitoring and reporting framework and introduces the use of key performance indicators. The effectiveness of forbearance measures should be evaluated periodically and the creditworthiness of borrowers should be re-assessment based on stress credit ratings and internal behavioral systems. Short-term: arrears capitalization; arrears repayment plan; reduced payment above interest only; interest only; reduced payment below interest only and grace period. Long-term: interest rate reduction; loan term extension; split balance; partial debt forgiveness/write-down; operational restructuring and debt to equity swap. Resolution and closure solutions: other out-of-court settlements; voluntary surrender; mortgage to rent/lease; voluntary sale of property; settlement of loans; loan sale; auction-collateral repossession; auction-collateral liquidation; closure via bankruptcy process and full debt write-off.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
The Law 4261/2014 transposes into Greek legislation the Directive 2013/36/EU on access to the activity of credit institutions and the prudential supervision of credit institutions and investment firms (known as Basel III). This Law deactivates the previous Law 3601/2007 and its corresponding amendments introduced by Laws 4021/2011 and 4172/2013, respectively.  According to the provisions of this Law, the Bank of Greece is the responsible authority to go into the special liquidation procedure when the license of a credit institution is revoked. In addition, the Bank of Greece appoints the Special Liquidator and supervises the overall liquidation procedures. The Special Liquidator is mandated to take over the management of failing credit institutions. In addition, the Bank of Greece has the right to mandate the appointed Liquidator to transfer assets owned by credit institution under special liquidation procedure to other credit institutions or bridge banks. The transfer of assets aims to safeguard financial stability and enhance public confidence in the domestic financial system. 
The Special Liquidation Committee - SLC (that was established in accordance with the provisions of Law 4172/2013) should be composed by five members, appointed by the Bank of Greece. The term of office is set for a 3-year time period, renewable only once for up to three more years. 
The special liquidator is obligated to seek SLC’s consensus for the following: 
a) Reconciliations of loan obligations valued higher than € 20.000. The reconciliations concern the partial debt forgiveness of loan principals. 
b) Restructurings of loan obligations valued higher than € 250.000, both performing and non-performing. The restructurings may concern the extension of loan repayment period or reduction of loan interest rates. 
c) Auctions of real estate properties. The consensus of SLC is not required if the tax value of the property is less than € 150.000 and the first strike price exceeds the 7/10ths of the accounting value. 
d) Auctions of loans, equities, bonds, corporate shares and other holdings. The consensus of SLC is not required if the accounting value is less than € 150.000 and if the first strike price exceeds the 7/10ths of the accounting value or if the securities are listed on a regulated market. 
The unanimous decision of SLC is required for loan reconciliations and restructurings and auctions of assets valued more than € 1.000.000.

description: This new Law amends the provisions of Law 4224/2013 which foresees the establishment of the “Governing Council for Private Debt Management”. More specifically, this Law amendment extends the scope of the previous Law in order to include the branches of foreign banks and other financial institutions such as financial holding companies, mixed financial holding companies, asset management companies and payment institutions. In addition, the Bank of Greece is designated as the responsible authority for supervising both the implementation of the “Code of Conduct” and establishment of comprehensive and effective systems for the resolution of non-performing debt of households, corporations and legal entities. In this context, the Bank of Greece may require financial institutions to take the necessary corrective measures and impose sanctions, administrative or penalties.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Code of Conduct on NPL management was initially introduced by Bank of Greece at end-December 2014. The Code of Conduct provided guidelines regarding the interaction of credit institutions with borrowers in arrears, based on an arrears resolution process which followed five steps: communication with debtor, information gathering, financial assessment, proposal of resolution solutions and objections handling process.  In parallel, the Code of Conduct introduced the concept of the “cooperative borrower”, financial assessment criteria, key elements of resolution proposals and an established policy on handling hardship and sensitive cases.

description: The Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) sets a new level for LTV loans at 80% instead of 75%. Thus, a risk weight of 35% is applied for mortgages with an LTV ratio below 80%. For the portion of loans that exceed a 80% LTV ratio based on market values, the risk weight is formed at 75% for retail customers.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Deferred tax assets (DTAs) might be converted to deferred tax credits (DTCs) under certain conditions. More specifically, DTAs related to: unamortized losses resulting from the participation in PSI and provisions for impairment of loans existing on 31 December 2014 and included in the Financial Statement of the respective year may be converted into DTCs. These conversion rights attributable to the Greek State correspond to common shares of total market value representing 110% of the non-offset able DTCs. For the purpose of the conversion, the institutions' market share price is the weighted average stock exchange price over the last 30 working days prior to the date when the above tax credit becomes a receivable.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
The Law 4307/2014 enables SMEs and professionals to restructure existing debt obligations towards financial institutions, the Tax Authority and Social Security Organizations. It is required the applied SMEs and personal businesses to be viable and had a turnover up to €2.500.000 for the financial year 2013. The corporate loans should be classified as NPEs, meaning they should be at least 90 days overdue and should amount up to the limit of €500.000 per financial institution. The loan restructurings or write-offs should be decided at the discretion of each financial institution based on criteria for assessing the repayment capacity of the borrower. The borrower is deprived of the benefits of the loan agreement if he delays more than three monthly installments. 
Apart from the above Out-of-Course process, the Law also foresees a judicial process, subject to the provision that the majority of the creditors (50,1%) consent to the restructuring plan; the Court Decision will be binding for all other creditors. Again, the borrower is deprived of the benefits of the Court Decision if he delays more than three monthly installments. 
The Law also foresees provisions for a special liquidation process, where creditors who represent the 40% of the total value of corporate debts may recourse to the Court in order to compensate from the liquidation of company’s assets.

The LCR shall be equal to the ratio of a credit institution’s liquidity buffer to its net liquidity outflows over a 30 calendar day stress period and shall be expressed as a percentage. Credit institutions shall maintain a liquidity coverage ratio of at least 60%.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The EU Commission published the Regulation (EU) No 2015/227, which sets out a harmonized definition of non-performing and forborne exposures. This Regulation is based on draft implementing technical standards submitted by the EBA to the Commission. The EBA has drafted these definitions and templates in application of Article 99(4) of Regulation EU No 575/2013 (CRR). The new definition builds on the definitions of impairment and default according to International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), while being broader than these notions with the setting of common identification and discontinuation criteria (90 days past-due) to serve as a more harmonized asset quality indicator across Europe. The new definition of non-performing exposures includes the defaulted and impairment exposures.

It also provides modifications in reporting requirements and templates, as a result, the new quarterly NPEs reporting framework contains detailed information on portfolio segmentation, collateral, legal workout activities, flows of non-performing exposures, sector distribution of business loans and performance of forbearance measures and closure solutions.

These money transfers abroad are permitted subject to the restrictions that the same transfers had been conducted prior to the imposition of capital controls measures or in the case of new investments, that these are funded from money remittances from abroad.
In addition, funds which are currently invested abroad are permitted to be re-invested. This rule concerns investment conducted by Undertakings for the Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS); AFM; Investment Funds; Insurance companies; Occupational and Pension Funds.  The lift of restrictions for money transfers domestically or abroad of banking institutions includes the conduct of interbank transactions; the settlement and clearing of securities; transactions with CCPs and repositories; the management of financial positions such as derivatives and foreign exchange; the payment of coupons, invoices or other contracts; nostro-vostro accounts. This lift of restrictions is permitted for the smooth functioning of operations and management of liquidity issues and does not concern transactions on behalf of customers of credit institutions, in any case.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
This new Law amendment extends the scope of the previous Law 3869/2010 so as the process of restructuring existing debt obligations to include all kind of debts, not just debts towards banks and financial institutions but also debts towards public funds, such as taxes and debts to the State, Municipalities and Social Security Organizations. It should be noted that these two kinds of debts is required to coexist. 
The Court now determines the monthly installment that the borrower has to pay to his creditors, after taking into account the “reasonable living expenses” of the debtor’s family (instead of the previous assessment of the financial situation of the borrower after taking into account his family needs). In any case, the new monthly installment should not be set lower than the 10% of the sum of the previous installments of all creditors, which should not be less than €40 and will be distributed to the creditors proportionally. However, if the borrower delays three monthly installments, the Court may declare his forfeiture from the settlement, after creditors’ such request. The Law also foresees the possibility of zero amount installments for borrowers who are completely unable to repay their loans, due to chronic unemployment or very serious health problems.
In addition, this Law amendment foresees the introduction of a new process for the settlement of small debt obligations up to the limit of €20.000, subject to the provisions that the borrower hadn’t earned any income over the last year, has no real estate property, his deposits and securities are up to the limit of €1.000 and the borrower is characterized as “cooperative borrower”. The last prerequisite ensures that the creditors and the Court have current and accurate information for the financial situation of the borrower and deters strategic defaulters. In such cases, the Court may decide to relieve the borrower from his debt obligations temporarily for a surveillance period of 18 months and consequently, the borrower will be relieved permanently if the same prerequisites are still met.  
The final Court decision may rule the liquidation of borrower’s assets and if the estimated value is not adequate to cover the outstanding amount then the Court will determine monthly installment for a period of three years (instead of the previous three to five years), covering the sum of debt obligations, which will be proportionally distributed to the creditors. The imposed installment for debt service will be based on the “reasonable living expenses” of the debtor’s family (instead of the previous assessment of the financial situation of the borrower after taking into account his family needs).
Protection of the main residence: This Law amendment provides protection for the main residence of the debtor to be exempted from the liquidation process, subject to new prerequisites which will be determined and will be based on the tax value of the property, the sum of the debt obligations and the family income of the debtor (instead of the previous criterion where the main residence should not exceed the size set by the tax laws for the acquisition of first residence, plus a premium of 50%).
 The interest should be equal to the one set for performing exposures, or the average floating interest rate for mortgages with reference rate the ECB main refinancing operations (MRO), or the average fixed interest rate for mortgages and without compounding rate. 
Finally, this new Law amendment foresees same changes in the judicial process, regarding the time frame of the Court hearings.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
The Law 4354/2015 foresees the establishment of (a) credit servicing firms and (b) credit acquiring firms in Greece for addressing the NPEs issue. These firms shall be specialized in NPEs management, namely legal and accounting monitoring, collection of installments, conduct of negotiations with debtors, loan reconciliations and restructurings and refinancing of existing loans. The only difference lies on the ownership status of loan contracts, meaning credit servicing firms do not acquire the ownership of NPEs they manage, in contrast with credit acquiring firms. 
These firms may be headquartered in Greece or in any other member-state of the European Economic Area (EEA), subject to the provision that foreign entities are legally established in Greece through branches. The share capital of  credit  acquiring firms should always exceed the limit of €100.000. The Bank of Greece is the competent supervisory authority for financial stability purposes and has the right to impose administrative fines up to the limit of €300.000 for specific violations.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description:
This new Law amendment balances creditors’ rights with a limited protection of vulnerable borrowers. 
Protection of the main residence: new prerequisites are set for the exemption of the main residence of the borrower from the liquidation process, until end-December 2018. Thus, the main residence is protected subject to the provisions that the family disposable income is up to the level of the “reasonable living expenses” increased by 70%, the tax value of the main residence should not exceed €180.000 for single persons, €220.000 for married couples, €240.000 for families with one child, €260.000 for families with two children, €280.000 for families with three or more children and the borrower is characterized as a “cooperative borrower”.  The borrower should pay a new monthly installment up to the maximum limit of his financial capacity so as creditors not to be worst-off compared with the liquidation proceeds (the present value of the borrower repayment plan is higher than the proceeds of a forced liquidation of the main residence). 
Especially, a borrower has the possibility to apply to the Greek State until end-December 2018, in order to benefit from a partial coverage of the new monthly installment (subsidy), subject to the provisions that the exempted from liquidation process residence is the main residence, the family disposable income is lower or up to the level of the “reasonable living expenses”, the tax value of the main residence should not exceed €120.000 for single persons, €160.000 for married couples, €180.000 from families with one child, €200.000 for families with two children, €220.000 for families with three or more children, the borrower is characterized as a “cooperative borrower” and is effectively defaulted, so he cannot pay the new monthly installment set by the Court. In any case, creditors should not be worst-off compared with the liquidation proceeds (the present value of the borrower repayment plan is higher than the proceeds of a forced liquidation of the main residence). In this framework, the Greek State will have to partially cover the new monthly installment directly to the creditors and the borrower will have to pay the rest of the installment, up to the limit of his payment capacity. The contribution of the Greek State should not exceed the three years period subject to the provision that the borrower will remain consistent to his financial liabilities. 
The borrower is deprived of the benefits of the temporary Court Decision if he delays three monthly installments. This encourages a prudent repayment culture.
The property of the borrower which is not exempt from confiscation (real estate properties except from the main residence) will be forfeited and disposed for the financial satisfaction of creditors.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
The Law B/717/2016 comes as a follow-up of the Banking Law 4261/2014 to specify issues regarding the legal framework of the special liquidation procedure. More specifically, the Special Liquidator is mandated to manage the  special liquidation procedures as a whole and he is supervised by the Bank of Greece. The Special Liquidator role could be assigned to a physical or a legal person. In addition, a new independent Audit Committee is established to supervise the liquidation procedures and assess the adequacy of the internal corporate governance system.
The Special Liquidator should inform the Bank of Greece for the reconciliations and restructurings of loan obligations that he signs at his discretion. Moreover, the Special Liquidator needs the Bank of Greece’s approval in order to dissolve subsidiaries, as holdings of the failing institutions under liquidation.
Finally, in cases whereas the liquidation procedure exceeds a five-year term, then the Special Liquidator shall submit to the Bank of Greece a plan for the acceleration and completion of the liquidation process.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The Law 4389/2016 modifies some of the provisions of the previous Law 4354/2015, regarding the establishment and operational framework of (a) credit servicing firms and (b) credit  acquiring firms for addressing the NPEs issue. More specifically, these firms may be headquartered in Greece or in any other member-state of the European Economic Area (EEA) and in addition, the new Law foresees the establishment of firms which may be branches of financial institutions headquartered in third countries, subject to the provisions of the European legal framework. Moreover, the share capital of credit servicing firms, which are licensed to grant new loans or credit provisions to borrowers who wish to refinance or restructure existing loans or credit provisions,  is set at €4.500.000. Credit servicing firms are obligated to present to the Bank of Greece alternative options for the restructuring of loans and have to exhaust all other options until they proceed to foreclosures, taking into account the European and Greek legal framework for the protection of borrowers, especially for the protection of socially vulnerable groups. In addition, the new Law foresees a grace period until end-December 2017 for residential real estate loans granted for the purchase of the main residence of the borrower, subject to the provision that the tax value of the property should not exceed the limit of €140.000.

description: The measure ensures for clients to participate in a scheme that alleviete the debt service (the size of monthly installments) by establishing an accumulation account that collects the debt burden depending on the difference between the preferential FX rate and the markat FX rate.  The exchange rate cap a tool capable to temporarily decrease debt servicing burdens of clients. Debtors of performing FX loans may apply for participation in the scheme until the end of 2011, pursuant to which they may repay their loans at preferential rates (HUF/CHF 180, HUF/EUR 250, HUF/JPY 2) during the period of the exchange rate fix lasting until the end of 2014. In this scheme, debtors with defaults not exceeding 90 days could make repayments for three years at a fixed, discounted exchange rate while the difference is charged to a forint pool account and incurs forint interest at a forint interest rate. This results in a prompt and significant decrease repayment, even though the decrease is temporary. Once the fixed exchange rate period is over, the debtor is required to repay both the loan accumulated on the pool account and the foreign exchange loan at the market exchange rate again.

description: Payment service providers, credit institutions authorized to pursue currency exchange activities and special services intermediaries of currency exchange services having a registered office or branch in the territory of Hungary have to pay financial transaction duty on payment transactions, including operations other than payment transactions. (1) The basis of assessment of the financial transaction duty shall be: (a) subject to the exceptions set out in Paragraphs b)-g), the sum deducted by the payment service provider from the payers payment account by order of the payer or the payee; (b) in the case of money remittance, the sum remitted; (c) in the case of cash deposits made through the institution operating the Posta Elszámoló Központ, the sum transferred to the payees payment service provider; (d) in the case of loan repayment, the sum debited to the clients payment account by the payment service provider; (e) in the case of cash withdrawal by way of a cash-substitute payment instrument, the sum withdrawn; (f) in connection with currency exchange activities by credit institutions authorized to pursue currency exchange activities and by special services intermediaries of currency exchange services, the amount of the payment instrument sold; (g) in connection with commissions and fees, the sum debited to the clients payment account by the payment service provider, or the sum charged with respect to the cash-substitute payment instrument. (2) In connection with payment orders, loan repayment transactions, charging commissions and fees and currency exchange activities executed in a foreign currency, the sum specified in Subsection (1) shall be translated to forints by the official MNB exchange rate in effect on the transaction date. The amount of financial transaction duty to be charged shall be: (a) 0.2 per cent of the financial transaction duty base, but not exceeding 6,000 forints per payment transaction; (b) subject to the exception set out in Paragraph d), 0.2 per cent of the financial transaction duty base, if the duty is payable by the institution operating the Posta Elszámoló Központ or the treasury; (c) 0.3 per cent of the financial transaction duty base in the case of cash withdrawal from a payment account, or in the case of cash withdrawal by way of a cash-substitute payment instrument, but not exceeding 6,000 forints per payment transaction; (d) 0.2 per cent of the financial transaction duty base, but not exceeding 6,000 forints per payment transaction in connection with payment transactions related to the distribution of government securities, if the duty is payable by the treasury.

description: Due to the excessive currency mismatch, the banks' dependency on the off-balance sheet instruments (typically on the swap market) is rather high, which may generate systemic risks through the significant refinancing, liquidity and margin call risks. Since FFAR – as follows from its nature – is not able to influence the entire spectrum of the on-balance sheet currency mismatch, the regulatory response to be given to the risks is built on two pillars, namely, on the modification of the foreign exchange funding adequacy ratio (FFAR), and the introduction of a new macroprudential requirement, managing the risks arising from the currency mismatch of assets and liabilities, i.e. the foreign exchange coverage ratio (FECR). A new tool is designed to manage the risks arising from the on-balance sheet denomination currency and the excessive dependence on the swap market. In order to take account of the differences arising from the size of the institutions, the foreign currency equilibrium ratio (FCER) would limit the onbalance sheet currency mismatch in 15 per cent in proportion to the balance sheet total.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Parliament transposed the CRDIV into its legal framework on 23 December 2013 by the Act of CCXXXVII on credit institutions and financial enterprises. In October 2015, the MNB’s Financial Stability Board decided to introduce the systemic risk buffer (SRB) in order to adequately manage risks arising from problem CRE exposures. The rate of the SRB will be set in proportion to the individual insitutions’ contribution to systemic risk. This rate is derived from the ratio of problem project loans to the domestic Pillar 1 capital requirement (if the ratio below 30 per cent the SRB rate is 0 per cent, if between 30-60 per cent the SRB rate 1 per cent, if between 60-90 per cent the SRB rate 1.5 per cent, if above 90 per cent the SRB rate 2 per cent. The SRB determined based on this ratio will be applied individually, between 1 and 2 per cent of total domestic risk-weighted assets, and credit institutions will be required to build it up at consolidated level, from Common Equity Tier 1 capital (CET1), in addition to other capital buffers. A ‘de minimis’ threshold has also been introduced in order to take into account systematically relevant assets: institutions with problem project exposures below HUF 5 billion are exempted from the SRB requirement.

The capital buffers: OTP Bank Nyrt. 2.00%, UniCredit Bank Hungary Zrt. 1.00%, Kereskedelmi és Hitelbank Zrt. 1.00%, Magyar Takarékszövetkezeti Bank Zrt. .50%, Raiffeisen Bank Zrt. 0.50%, Erste Bank Hungary Zrt. 0.50%, CIB Bank Zrt. 0.50%, MKB Bank Zrt. 0.50% will be phased- in between 2017 and 2020. description: The Parliament transposed the CRDIV into its legal framework on 23 December 2013 by the Act of CCXXXVII on credit institutions and financial enterprises. This is the base for the introduction of the countercyclical capital buffer regime. The current CCB rate for the Hungarian exposures and the relevant conditions are set by MNB Decrees. By the MNB Decree 57/2015. (XII. 22.). the CCB rate was set at 0 per cent in effect from 1 January 2016.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Parliament transposed the CRDIV into its legal framework on 23 December 2013 by the Act of CCXXXVII on credit institutions and financial enterprises. The MNB identified the following entities as other systemically important institutions (O-SIIs) in 2015: OTP Bank Nyrt, Kereskedelmi és Hitelbank Zrt., UniCredit Bank Hungary Zrt., Erste Bank Hungary Zrt., Raiffeisen Bank Zrt., Magyar Takarékszövetkezeti Bank Zrt., MKB Bank Zrt., CIB Bank Zrt., FHB Jelzálogbank Nyrt.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Modification of the scope of LTV limits for car loans denominated in domestic currency. The limit remains 75% LTV on HUF car loans, 80% on financial leasing. The "de minimis" limit has been raised: in the future, the loan amount below which it is not necessary to apply the regulation will increase from 200,000 forints to 300,000 forints. This modification also reduces the consumers' administrative burdens.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Modification of the scope of LTV limits for new mortgage loans  denominated in foreign currencies. The limit remains at 50% LTV on EUR, 35% LTV on other FX exposures. In case of financial leasing 55% on EUR, 40% on other currency. The LTV cap applies to new mortgage loans for all purpose. The "de minimis" limit has also been raised: in the future, the loan amount below which it is not necessary to apply the regulation will increase from 200,000 forints to 300,000 forints. This modification also reduces the consumers' administrative burdens.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Banks must adopt and apply internal rules to  examine the creditworthiness and monthly maximum debt service capacity (loanability limit) of the potential borrowers . The limits are differentiated according to the currency of the loan and the net income of the borrower (<=, > HUF 400,000). PTI for (1) monthly income below HUF 400,000: 25% for EUR, 10% for other FX lending (2) montly income of HUF 400,000 and above: 30% for EUR, 15% for other FX lending. In the future, the instalments of the mortgage loans with an interest period of at least five years can be taken into account in the payment-to-income ratio with a preferential, 85 per cent weight, thereby supporting the spreading of mortgage loans with longer interest periods, bearing lower interest risk. In addition, upon increasing the limit of credit facilities at the customer's request within three years on the first occasion in each calendar year, it will not be necessary to submit an income certificate in case of problem-free cases, thereby reducing the administrative burdens of the consumers.  The "de minimis" limit has also been raised: in the future, the loan amount below which it is not necessary to apply the regulation will increase from 200,000 forints to 300,000 forints. This modification also reduces the consumers' administrative burdens.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Modification of PTI limits. The limits for HUF loans are differentiated according to the net income of the borrower (<=, > HUF 400,000). PTI for (1) monthly income below HUF 400,000: 50% for HUF (2) monthly income of HUF 400,000 and above: 60% for HUF. In the future, the instalments of the mortgage loans with an interest period of at least five years can be taken into account in the payment-to-income ratio with a preferential, 85 per cent weight, thereby supporting the spreading of mortgage loans with longer interest periods, bearing lower interest risk. The "de minimis" limit has also been raised: in the future, the loan amount below which it is not necessary to apply the regulation will increase from 200,000 forints to 300,000 forints. This modification also reduces the consumers' administrative burdens.

description: Modification of the scope of LTV limits for car loans denominated in foreign currencies: 45% LTV on EUR, 30% LTV on other FX exposures. In case of financial leasing 50% on EUR, 35% on other currency. The "de minimis" limit has also been raised: in the future, the loan amount below which it is not necessary to apply the regulation will increase from 200,000 forints to 300,000 forints. This modification also reduces the consumers' administrative burdens.

The LTV cap applies to new mortgage loans for all purpose. category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The MNB’s Financial Stability Board has modified the Mortgage Loan Financing Adequacy Ratio (MFAR) requirement's date of entry into force from 1 October 2016 to 1 April 2017, in order to ensure that credit institutions are able to comply with the mortgage funding requirements under the new mortgage rules.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool

The MNB identified the following entities as other systemically important institutions in 2016: OTP Bank Nyrt, UniCredit Bank Hungary Zrt., Kereskedelmi és Hitelbank Zrt., Magyar Takarékszövetkezeti Bank Zrt.,Raiffeisen Bank Zrt., Erste Bank Hungary Zrt.,CIB Bank Zrt.,MKB Bank Zrt..

action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: In September 2016, the MNB’s Financial Stability Board decided to postpone the introduction of the systemic risk buffer (SRB) in order to promote soft adjustment of banks via portfolio cleansing relating to problem CRE exposures. Banks in focus has to maintain SRB from 1 July 2017 based on 31 March 2016 position. Other conditions remained unchanged.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: This is the first regulatory document on impairment provisions, which covers both specific and general provisions. The paper set out the requirements and supervisory perspective of the Irish Central Bank with regard to the policies and procedures to be adopted by credit institutions for credit loss provisioning. This document expands on the high level principles outlined in section 8.1 of the Licensing and Supervision Requirements and Standards for Credit Institutions in relation to provisioning. This policy paper is divided into two parts, the first part contains qualitative requirements on credit risk management and impairment provisioning while the second part of the paper documents the Financial Regulator’s perspective on impairment provisioning setting out quantitative criteria and reporting guidelines.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Commission Regulation (EC) 1864/2005 became directly applicable in Ireland in 2005. This Regulation carved out the Fair Value Option and the Macro Hedging elements of IAS 39.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The weighting of new Irish residential mortgages was amended with effect from 1 May 2006 such that mortgages that exceed 80 per cent of the value of the property (except to the extent that such excess is covered by third party insurance) attracted a risk weighting of 100 per cent for the portion of the mortgage in excess of 80 per cent at the inception of the loan.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Discretion under Para 66 Annex VI CRD to risk weight speculative commercial real estate in Ireland at 150% was implemented. These loans were defined as loans for the purposes of:(i) land or building acquisitions; or (ii) development or construction in relation to such property. Such lending ceased to be considered speculative if a level of contracted pre-sales or pre-letting of at least 50% of the property (by value) was achieved. Furthermore, such exposures were not be treated as speculative to the extent that an institution had recourse to contract: (i) alternative sources of cash flow; (ii) other realisable security.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Without prejudice to points 9, 10 and 11 (Annex VI, Part 1, Section 2 CRD 2006/48/EC) exposures to regional governments and local authorities shall be risk-weighted as exposures to institutions, subject to point 11a (same Annex). Such treatment is independent of the exercise of discretion specified in Article 80(3) CRD 2006/48/EC. The preferential treatment for short-term exposures specified in points 31, 32 and 37 shall not be applied.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: CRE was risk weighted at 100% under the Solvency Directive in EU (implementing Basel 1).  With the introduction of CRD in 2006 the CBI availed of discretions provided under CRD regarding secured mortgage exposures.  Under para. 51 of the same Annex the CBI did not exercise the discretion for CRE to permit 50% risk weight and a 100% risk weight applied.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: RRE was risk weighted at 50% under the Solvency Directive in EU (implementing Basel 1).  With the introduction of CRD in 2006 the CBI applied the following measures and availed of discretions provided under CRD regarding secured mortgage exposures.  In accordance with Para 49, Annex VI, Part 1, the CBI provided that loans with an LTV not higher than 75% would attract a 35% risk weight, the amount of any exposure above 75% LTV would attract a risk weight of 75% if the exposure met the definition of the retail exposure class under Article 79(2) of Directive 2006/48/EC.  Otherwise a 100% risk weight was to apply.  Where institutions did not record current LTVs they could use either (i) original LTVs or (ii) original LTVs adjusted by an appropriate index, which takes into account geographical and house type factors.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Amendment to IAS 39 to permit reclassification of debt and equity financial instruments out of Fair Value Through Profit and Loss (FVTPL) and Available for Sale. Those insturments designated as at FVTPL on itital recognition under the 'fair value option' cannot be reclassifed. The purpose of the amendment was to create a level playing field with US GAAP regarding the ability to reclassify financial assets.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch

description: Introduction of the limit requiring that liquid assets should cover 90% net outflows out to 30 days.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
subcategory: Short-term liquidity coverage ratios incl. Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Introduction of the limit requiring that liquid assets should cover 100% net outflows out to 8 days.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Introduction of a set of qualitative requirements for the management of liquidity risk. These relate to inter alia risk management, corporate governance, stress testing and contingency funding planning.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Central Bank imposed conditions on banks’ licences in August 2009 requiring them to disclose in their annual audited accounts all lending to ‘connected persons’ in aggregate and the maximum liability during the year. The Central Bank’s condition was more onerous than what applied in the Companies Acts in that it extended the public disclosures to all lending to connected persons of directors and not just lending on favourable terms.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: If a client, or a group of connected clients is (a) the parent undertaking of a credit institution, (b) a subsidiary or subsidiaries of that undertaking, (c) a subsidiary or subsidiaries of the institution, or (d) comprises any 2 or more such entities, the institution may not incur an exposure to the client or group that exceeds 20% of its own funds.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Exposures to a client or group of connected clients, other than a credit institution, in which the credit institution has a significant shareholding should remain below 5% of own funds.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The aggregate of exposures to a client or group of connected clients, other than a credit institution, in which the credit institution has a significant shareholding should remain below 15% of own funds.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The RPL Code was issued in October 2010 and came in force on 1 January 2011. It was introduced to seek to prevent abuses arising from exposures to related parties. It included the definitions of a related party, significant shareholder, connected persons. RPL Code applies only to lending (loans, quasi-loans or credit transactions which results in an exposure or potential exposure, including guarantees) to related parties. There is a provision for application for exemptions to lending limits for certain intrgroup lending.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In March 2011 the Financial Measures Programme (FMP) stipulated that 4 banks (AIB, BOI, EBS and ILP) should move towards a LDR target of 122.5 per cent by December 2013.  A number of six-monthly, non-public, interim LDR targets were set to ensure satisfactory progress. Banks were also required to submit detailed plans on a semi-annual basis outlining how the next interim target would be achieved.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Deactivation of an existing tool
description: The limit on ten largest deposits (including interbank) of credit institutions of 50% of total deposits were discussed as obsolete during June 2011.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Deactivation of an existing tool
description: The limit imposed on credit institutions that they may not owe more than 15 per cent of total deposits (including interbank) to any one depositor or what is deemed by the Central Bank of Ireland to be an associated group of depositors was repealed.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The Central Bank issued Impairment Provisioning and Disclosure Guidelines in 2011 which are considered best practice guidelines to support credit institutions in the development and application of their impairment frameworks under IAS 39. The 2011 Guidelines encouraged banks to be more conservative in their provisioning and to have higher quality disclosures than the earlier document on provisioning from 2005.  While remaining within the confines of IFRS the Central Bank was more prescriptive in its views of what constituted best practice.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In September 2012 following agreement with the EC-ECB-IMF, FMP banks were informed by the Central Bank that the LDR targets would be replaced by a non-core deleveraging target amount and a requirement to establish an Advanced Monitoring Framework (AMF) The AMF aims to re-orientate banks’ strategies, processes and governance towards fulfilment of new Basel III liquidity requirements, which will be introduced under the EU Credit Requirements Directive/Regulation IV. The Central Bank will monitor each bank’s progress towards achieving the minimum levels of both the NSFR and the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) by their respective implementation dates of 1 January 2018 and 1 January 2015 .  Quarterly reporting requirements for this issue were also prescribed by the Central Bank. The Bank established an advanced monitoring framework covering all factors affecting banks’ Net Stable Funding Ratio, to enable closer monitoring of progress towards meeting these Basel III requirements.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Mortgage Arrears Resolution Targets (MART) sets out a framework for setting performance targets for mortgage arrears resolution for the specified Irish mortgage credit institutions. Includes specific targets which  cover both proposed and concluded sustainable solutions with respect to the lenders’ Republic of Ireland principal dwelling home / primary residence (‘PDH’) and buy-to-let (‘BTL’) mortgagees, and specifically centres on resolving arrears cases which are 90 days or more overdue. A sustainable solution has been proposed to mortgage holders with % target quarter on quarter for 4Q 2013 set at 50% with suggested guideline targets for the preceeding quarters

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: The Mortgage Arrears Resolution Targets (MART) sets out a framework for setting performance targets for mortgage arrears resolution for the specified Irish mortgage credit institutions.  The final goal level in the public goals section refers to agreement being in place and the mortgage holder in arrears adhering to the agreed terms (making their repayments). This goal was set for 75% from Q1 2014 onwards. Public targets are supplemented with institutional targets which are set with each individual credit institution reflecting their capacity, processes and systems. They are dynamic and adjusted quarterly to ensure that the targets are ambitious. These targets will primarily monitor early arrears cases and operational effectiveness.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Final fully-phased Tier 1 capital ratio of 6% (CRR Art 92, 1(b))

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The Central Bank issued revised Impairment Provisioning and Disclosure Guidelines in 2013. The revision includes definitions of non-performing loans and 'cured loans' and the guidelines are recommended for use by credit insitutions in their financial annual reports.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: An institution shall not incur an exposure, after taking into account the effect of the credit risk mitigation in accordance with Articles 399 to 403, to a client or group of connected clients the value of which exceeds 25 % of its eligible capital. Where that client is an institution or where a group of connected clients includes one or more institutions, that value shall not exceed 25 % of the institution's eligible capital or EUR 150 million, whichever the higher, provided that the sum of exposure values, after taking into account the effect of the credit risk mitigation in accordance with Articles 399 to 403, to all connected clients that are not institutions does not exceed 25 % of the institution's eligible capital. Where the amount of EUR 150 million is higher than 25 % of the institution's eligible capital the value of the exposure, after taking into account the effect of credit risk mitigation in accordance with Articles 399 to 403 shall not exceed a reasonable limit in terms of the institution's eligible capital. That limit shall be determined by the institution in accordance with the policies and procedures referred to in Article 81 of Directive 2013/36/EU, to address and control concentration risk. This limit shall not exceed 100 % of the institution's eligible capital.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Final fully-phased Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5% (CRR Art 92, 1(a))

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Under Article 465(1)(a) of CRR, the Central Bank was entitled to determine the phase-in rate for Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1). Institutions, therefore, were required to hold a minimum level of CET1 of 4% from 1 January 2014.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Art. 92 CRR stipulates min CAR as a total capital ratio of 8%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Under Article 465(1)(a) of CRR, the Central Bank was entitled to determine the phase-in rate for Tier 1 regulatory ratio. Institutions, therefore, were required to hold a minimum level of Tier 1 of 5.5% from 1 January 2014.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Revision of the RPL Code that was issued in May 2010 in 2013 to update if for some issues identified by the Banking industry with regard to the implementation of the 2010 Code as follows: (i) Debt for Equity Swaps, (ii) Definition of Connected Persons and Clients, (iii) De Minimis Limits, (iv) Definition of Control within the Definition of Connected Persons and Clients, (v) Exemptions on Intra-Group Transactions.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: The Central Bank availed of the discretion under Article 124(2) of CRR not to allow a reduced risk weighting of 50% for CRE exposures. A minimum RW of 100% on CRE exposures applies.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
The Central Bank availed of the discretion under Article 124(2) of CRR to set stricter criteria in this area. Accordingly, the Central Bank permitted a 35 per cent risk weighting for such exposures but only where the LTV at market value does not exceed 75 per cent and the residential property is owner-occupied and the other specified conditions are met. Any amount above 75 per cent LTV or exposure to a mortgage secured by residential property not meeting the conditions of Article 125 of CRR may attract a 75 per cent risk weighting. This is provided that the exposure meets certain conditions. These conditions include:
- that the relevant amount of the exposure does not exceed 1 million Euro in combination with all other owed amounts of exposures to the obligor or group of connected obligors (but not taking account of exposures actually treated as secured on real estate property); and
- that it satisfies the definition of ‘retail exposure class’ under Article 123 CRR.
A 75 per cent risk weighting can be assigned to exposures to mortgages secured by residential investment properties if the exposure meets the definition of retail exposure under Article 123 of CRR. Otherwise a 100 per cent risk weight applies.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Bank Levy was introduced by the department of Finance. Levied on all banks and imposed on the basis of scale of deposits held. The total cost of the levy was 150mil per year to run for three years. The contribution will be related to the amount of tax paid on deposit interest by the institutions in the calendar year 2011.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: Risk weight speculative commercial real estate in Ireland at 150% is no longer a discretion for the Central Bank to implement as it applies as standard treatment under CRR Art 128(2)(d); institutions shall assign a 150% risk weight to exposures on speculative immovable financing.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Deactivation of an existing tool
description: S.I. No. 158 of 2014 revokes the European Communities (Capital Adequacy of Credit Institutions) Regulations 2006 (S.I. No 6661 of 2006) which had incorporated the original large exposures limit of max 800% of own funds imposed via the Implementation of the EU Directive on the Monitoring and Control of Large Exposures of Credit Institutions (92/121/EEC of 21 December, 1992)

action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: The Central Bank  determined that relying on common quarterly solution targets across all banks was no longer appropriate.  The Central Bank has written to each bank setting out new requirements that: (i) concluded sustainable solutions are in place for the vast majority of distressed borrowers by the end of 2015; (ii) they meet the ‘terms being met’ target of 75 per cent of concluded solutions to the end of 2015 and beyond; (iii) they continue to comply with the Code of Conduct on Mortgage Arrears; (iv) where they  take legal action that may result in loss of ownership for a borrower, they should be prepared to re-engage with the borrower and explore alternative solutions if the borrower re-engages; and (v) they engage fully and appropriately in the process set out in the Personal Insolvency Act,  2012.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: The LTV threshold is 80 per cent for mortgages secured by residential property. Mortgages with LTVs above these thresholds can be granted, but those with LTVs below the thresholds benefit from a more favourable risk weighting. The value of the property is equal to the market value (or mortgage lending value) reduced if necessary to reflect the results of monitoring as well as any earlier mortgages on the property. The instrument has been introduced as a microprudential threshold but can be used for macroprudential purposes if needed.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Introduction of the operational risk into the definition of CAR. Bank of Italy Circular 27 December 2006, no. 263 - “New provisions on prudential supervision for banks” entered into force on 1/1/2007.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Bank of Italy Circular 27 December 2006, no. 263 - “New provisions on prudential supervision for banks” aimed at harmonizing the national legislation with the Basel II framework entered into force on 1/1/2007, introducing inter alia IRB based approach in the calculationof RWA.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: The LTV threshold is  50 per cent for mortgages secured by commercial real estate. Mortgages with LTVs above these thresholds can be granted, but those with LTVs below the thresholds benefit from a more favourable risk weighting. The value of the property is equal to the market value (or mortgage lending value) reduced if necessary to reflect the results of monitoring as well as any earlier mortgages on the property. The instrument has been introduced as a microprudential threshold but can be used for macroprudential purposes if needed.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: A total capital ratio of 8% (CRR Art 92, 1(c)) entered into force on 1/1/2014. There was a change in the scope of of this tool, as CRR introduced some tightening to the definition of capital and RWA.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 on prudential requirements for credit institutions and investment firms entered into force on 1/1/2014 stipulating minimum capital requirements:Tier 1 Capital ratio 6%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 on prudential requirements for credit institutions and investment firms entered into force on 1/1/2014 stipulating  minimum capital requirements: CET1 ratio 4,5%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Shorter transitional period. The buffer set to 2.5% of the total exposures. Small and medium-sized investment firms are exempted from the requirement.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Bank of Italy has identified UniCredit banking group as a global systemically important institution (G-SII) authorized to operate in Italy. According to the transition period envisaged under Directive 2013/36/EU (Capital Requirements Directive IV – CRD IV), the UniCredit group is required to maintain a capital buffer for the G-SIIs of an amount equal to 0.25 per cent of its total risk exposure from 1 January 2016. This buffer must be increased annually by 0.25 per cent of total risk exposure to reach 1 per cent of total risk exposure no later than 1 January 2019.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool

This buffer will be further increased by 0.25 per cent of total risk exposure annually to reach 1 per cent of total risk exposure no later than 1 January 2019.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool

category: Limits on credit growth and volume

subcategory: Other income requirements for loan eligibility
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: All lenders granting loans to households have to require an official verification of a consumer's income from the State Revenue Service if the amount of loan equals or exceeds 100 times minimum monthly wages.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Downpayment  in the amount of 10% of the purchased goods or services has been introduced for the loans issued for the purchase of goods and services. The requirement applies to the loans of the size which is 100 times minimum monthly wage or higher

action_type: Activation of a new tool

category: Limits on credit growth and volume

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The FCMC Regulations "On Credit Risk management" include the requirements for credit risk management. Among those are requirements to implement credit granting policy that covers credit granting criteria and limits, terms and limits for granting unsecured credits, criteria for assessment of borrowers creditworthiness, types of eligible collateral, limits on loan-to-value and others.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: According to the FCMC Regulations on Credit Risk Management the bank shall develop credit granting policy that inter alia includes internal debt service ratios for different types of borrowers, namely, proportion borrowers's debt sevicing expenses to total net income of the borrower over the relevant period of time. No specific quantitative limits are set.
