subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Following the implementation of CRD II, for exposures fully and completely secured by mortgages on commercial immovable property, a 50% risk weight shall be assigned to the part of the loan that does not exceed 50 % of the market value of the property or 60% of the mortgage lending value, whichever is lower. Above that limit a 100% risk weight is assigned. CSSF Circular 06/273 which transposes, inter alia, Directive 2009/111/EC (CRD II) into national law, requires institutions to assign a 50% RW to the following exposures: (i) exposures or any part of an exposure, fully secured by mortgages on offices or other commercial premises located in Luxembourg; (ii) exposures fully and completely secured by shares in Finnish residential housing companies, operating in accordance with the Finnish Housing Company Act of 1991 or subsequent equivalent legislation, in respect of offices or other commercial premises (in accordance with conform to the provisions introduced by Article 1, point 26  of CRDII); (iii) exposures to a property leasing transaction concerning offices or other commercial premises located in Luxembourg for which the credit institution is the lessor and the tenant has an option to purchase, provided that the exposure of the credit institution is fully and completely secured by its ownership of the property.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description:
Institutions applying the standardised approach changed the risk weights for loans backed up by RRE from 50% to 35%.
Circular 06/273 of 22 December 2006 transposed into national law the the CRD I package and required institutions using the standardised approach to apply a 35% risk weight on exposures or any part of an exposure fully and completely secured by mortgages on residential property which is or shall be occupied or let by the owner, or the beneficial owner in the case of personal investment vehicles.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: The large exposures regime, as previously provided in Circular CSSF 06/273, was relaxed by increasing the permissible limit on large exposures on to a client or a group of connected clients that is the parent undertaking or a subsidiary to 25% of own funds.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The CSSF monitors the development of the liquidity situation of banks through the new liquidity reportings as well as through the other existing prudential reportings and self-assessments to be provided in the context of ICAAP reports (Circular 07/301 of 17 July 2007) which must include an assessment on the materiality, the management and the mitigation of liquidity risk. Circular CSSF 07/301 transposes EU risk management rules into Luxembourg regulation and includes the general provisions applicable to the institutions' risk management which apply to all risks, including liquidity risks.

action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description:
Circular CSSF 08/340 of 21 February 2008 provides further details on the legal publication of accounts and is complementary to the Law of 17 June 1992.
The purpose of this circular is to:
 i) explain the changes introduced by the law of 16 March 2006 relating to the introduction of international accounting standards for credit institutions (“Law of 16 March 2006”);
ii) clarify certain issues related to the legal publication of accounts; and
iii) define the interaction between the accounting regime for the legal publication of accounts and the prudential reporting under IAS/IFRS
Moreover, this circular provides details in relation to the first-time application of IAS/IFRS standards to the prudential financial reporting.

action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: The CSSF exercised its power to request a specific use of the lump sum provisions built up in prior years. Circular CSSF 08/386 reminds the banks, as already referred in , that they must use their lump sum provision at the end of the financial year 2008 in order to cover the unrealised losses resulting from the turmoil in the financial markets. Relates to the accounts published under Lux GAAP.

subcategory: Other capital surcharges and own funds requirements
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Capital surcharge of 2% applied to the domestically-oriented banks issuing mortgage credits. The 2% surcharge was the result of a stress testing exercise conducted by CSSF showing that a severe downturn in the Luxembourg real estate market could potentially result in a capital depletion of up to 2%. With the implementation of CRDIV as per beginning of 2014, this was replaced by the capital conservation buffer of 2.5% for all banks.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Circular CSSF 09/403 specifies the implementation of Articles 5(1a) and 17(1a) of the Law of 5 April on the financial sector, as amended which requires Luxembourg credit institutions and investment firms to have effective processes to identify, manage, monitor and report the risks they are or might be exposed to. This Circular aims at transposing into national regulation the CEBS guidelines on sound liquidity risk management. which are based on the "Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision" published by the BCBS in September 2008.

action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: The CSSF exercised its power to request a specific use of the lump sum provisions built up in prior years. Circular CSSF 11/526 reminds the banks that they must use their lump sum provision at the end of the financial year 2011 in order to cover the unrealised losses resulting from the turmoil in the financial markets. Relates to the accounts published under Lux GAAP.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In 2011, EBA decided to require 71 European banking groups to comply with a 9% Core Tier 1 ratio as from July 2012 onwards (EBA/REC/2011/1). This recommendation directly applied to only one (domestic) bank in Luxembourg. To ensure a level playing field within the Luxembourg banking sector and after having analysed the situation of the banks that are not subject to the EBA’s decision, the CSSF decided to assess henceforth the capital adequacy of all Luxembourg banks according to a 9% Core Tier 1 ratio on a regular basis. The adoption of this recommendation had no impact on Luxembourg credit institutions’ capitalisation levels given that a large majority of the domestic banks (68%) already had a solvency ratio exceeding 15%.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In accordance with the joint circulars BCL 2012/230 and CSSF 12/538 of 29 June 2012, institutions shall identify, manage, monitor and internally report their funding and liquidity risks in connection with foreign currency lending, together with their overall liquidity positions. Particular attention should be paid to the risks related to: (i) concentrations of funding sources; (ii) the use of foreign currency swaps; (iii) maturity mismatches between foreign currency assets and liabilities; (iv) currency mismatches between assets and liabilities. In addition, credit institutions shall have in place risk strategies, policies and limits which determine their risk tolerance with respect to foreign currency liquidity and funding. The risk tolerance and the corresponding limits shall be commensurate with the bank’s risk bearing and risk management capacities and shall be enforced. This joint circulars to all credit institutions, investment firms and professionals carrying on lending operations that grant loans in foreign currencies.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Circular 12/552 of 11 December 2012 requires institutions using the standardised approach for credit risk to apply the preferential risk weight of 35% only to the parts of their mortgages whose loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is below 80% (mortgages "whose value of the property is at least 25% higher than that of the exposure").The part of the mortgage exceeding 80% of the value of the real estate object is to be weighted according to the underlying exposure class. In this particular instance, the exposure shall comply with all criteria for retail exposures and the risk weight shall consequently be 75%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Institutions using the internal ratings-based approach shall ensure that their regulatory capital adequacy is subject to a stress test which considers the effects of severe, but plausible, recession scenarii. Those credit institutions are required to perform stress tests on the retail exposures secured by residential property requiring an increase of minimum 50% of the PDs and a LGD of at least 20%. In addition, all credit institutions must respect qualitative requirements which include internal limits to exposures to real estate developers, fixation of a repayment date of certain credit exposures and prohibition of rolling over interest payments at maturity.

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: Following the CRR, for exposures fully and completely secured by mortgages on commercial immovable property, a 50% risk weight shall be assigned to the part of the loan that does not exceed 50 % of the market value of the property. Above that limit a 100% risk weight is assigned.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In accordance with Article 5 of the CSSF Regulation N° 14-01 on the implementation of certain discretions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 and Article 92 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, the Luxembourg institutions are required to observe, as of 1 January 2014, a Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5% (instead of 4%; CRR, Article 465). Unrealised gains arising from the fair value measurement shall not be included in the calculation of Common Equity Tier 1 in the years 2014 to 2017 (cf. Article 8).

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: In accordance with Article 5 of the CSSF Regulation N° 14-01 on the implementation of certain discretions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 and Article 92 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, the Luxembourg institutions are required to observe, as of 1 January 2014, a total capital ratio of 8%. Change on the scope of an existing tool: (i) some tightening to the definition of capital and RWA in line with CRR, (ii) loosening in areas, such as the preferential treatment of exposures to SME, less strict approach to exposures to some equity holdings, adding general provisions, cancellation of deduction of expected loss surplus over provisions for banks using standardised approach etc.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In accordance with Article 5 of the CSSF Regulation N° 14-01 on the implementation of certain discretions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 and Article 92 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, the Luxembourg institutions are required to observe, as of 1 January 2014, a Tier 1 capital ratio of 6%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Shorter transitional period. Credit institutions shall have a capital conservation buffer made up of Common Equity Tier 1 equal to 2.5% of the total amount of their risk exposure, calculated in accordance with Article 92(3) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 on an individual and consolidated basis. (CSSF Regulation 14-01, CRDIV, Article 129). With the implementation of the CRDIV, the capital surcharge of 2% applied to the domestically-oriented banks issuing mortgage credits was replaced by the capital conservation buffer of 2,5% for all banks. Until beginning of 2014, a capital surcharge of 2% was applied to the domestically-oriented banks issuing mortgage credits.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: CSSF Regulation N° 14-02 published on 9 January 2015 prohibits dividend payments and distribution of reserves based on unrealized gains. The Regulation relates to the determination of distributable results and reserves of credit institutions applying the fair value measurement in the statutory account. This CSSF Regulation applies the provisions of the new Article 72b/64h of the TCR Law to the credit institutions. It shall be read jointly with the provisions of Circular CSSF 08/340 (points I.2.3 and I.3.1) pursuant to which unrealised gains arising from the fair value measurement of certain balance sheet items and recognised in a revaluation reserve, are not distributable (qualified as unavailable), and with the provisions of CSSF Regulation N° 14-01 on the implementation of certain discretions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, pursuant to which unrealised gains arising from the fair value measurement shall not be included in the calculation of Common Equity Tier 1 in the years 2014 to 2017 (cf. Article 8).

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: In accordance with Article 33, 11°,(iii) which of the Law of 23 July 2015 which transposed into national law Article 113(1)(b) of the CRD IV, the permanent supervision of liquidity risk of banks belonging to cross-border banking groups at EU level has been explicitly integrated in the joint supervisory process of the colleges of supervisors. In this regard, an individual analysis of the liquidity situation of the banks is made within the framework of the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP), before taking a joint decision on the adequacy of liquidity management and liquidity reserves of credit institutions. Within the SSM, this process is internalised in the Joint Supervisory Teams (JST) which perform the prudential controls of the significant banks on a day-to-day basis. In addition, the CSSF performs on-site inspections in co-operation with the BCL in order to assess, in a detailed manner, the situation and management of the liquidity risk within credit institutions.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch

In Luxembourg, the LCR minimum requirement of 60% entered into force on 1 October 2015 as laid down in Circular 15/621 of 21/10/2015. 
The LCR is to be reported by all credit institutions established in Luxembourg, on an individual basis and on a consolidated basis, where appropriate.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Rule is modelled on the Recommendation of the European Systemic Risk Board on lending in foreign currencies (ESRB/2011/1) published as Notice No. 2011/C 342/01 of the Official Journal of the European Union, which was approved by the General Board of the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) on 21 September 2011, in accordance with Regulation (EU) No. 1092/2010.The goals of the ESRB Recommendations were: (i) to limit exposure to credit and market risks, thus increasing the resilience of the financial system; (ii) to control excessive foreign currency credit growth and avoid asset price bubbles; (iii) to limit funding and liquidity risks and (iv) to improve risk pricing.The scope of this Rule is to outline five principles regulating the conduct of foreign currency lending. These are the following: (1) Risk awareness of borrowers (2) Assess creditworthiness of borrowers in extending foreign currency loans (3) Internal risk management- institutions should account for risks stemming from foreign currency lendingas part of their risk managment (4) Capital requirements - hold adequate capital to cover risks associated with foreign currency lending (5) Liquidity and funding - institutions shall monitor funding and liquidity risks in connection with foreign currency lending

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Revision of BR/09. The Rule brought provisioning standards in line with IRFS and allocated additional capital to a reserve (Reserve for General Banking Risks). The objective is for credit institutions to build a capital buffer over and above provisions required by IAS 39, which is aimed at strengthening their loss absorbing capacity to address credit risk. The regulatory capital allocation is equal to 2.5% of a bank’s NPLs, less specific impairments (according to IFRS as adopted in the European Union) and interest in suspense. In the case of non-performing exposures with capital and/or interest past due by 24 months or more, the 2.5% metric shall, as a minimum, increase to 5%. The capital allocation is to be sourced from dividends distributable for the year. In case when a credit institution has total Common Equity Tier 1 capital (CET 1) as per Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) that exceeds a threshold determined by the authority, only half (50%) of the appropriation shall be allocated to the “Reserve for General Banking Risks” from the dividend to be distributed for the year.

The following are reported: the cash inflow and cash outflow over the following periods (1) the period of two months following the month period, (2) the period of three months following the period in 1. (3) the period of six months following the period in 2. (4) the period following on the period referred to under 3.

description: The minimum quantitative requirements are set on the basis of a standard reporting framework that was introduced in its original form in 2003. As from 1 May 2011, under the revised Supervisory Regulation on Liquidity (Regeling liquiditeit Wft) of October 2010, the calculation of required liquidity is subject to a number of revised weighting percentages and classification requirements, implying increased liquidity requirements. Moreover, individual institutions may be subjected to an additional liquidity requirement underlain by special features of their risk profile or risk management. Also, individual institutions may be subjected to the application of a minimum percentage of highly liquid assets relative to the total of liquid assets recognised in this context. The revised liquidity regulations constitute an intermediate step until, at the latest, the time when the standardised minimum requirements are introduced at the European level (CRD IV).

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: On 1 August 2011, the Code of Conduct was revised, which tightened mortgage lending. Interest-only mortgages were only allowed up to 50% of the market value of the house, where previously it had been possible to finance the entire purchase with an interest-only mortgage.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: On 1 August 2011, the Code of Conduct was revised, which tightened mortgage lending. Households were no longer permitted to borrow more than 104% of the home’s market value plus transfer tax. With the transfer tax having been reduced to 2% in July 2011, this rate stood at 106%. Earlier limit for the loan amount for new mortgages was comparable with 110%  i.e. standard of 125% of the foreclosure value, assuming the foreclosure value amounts to 90% of the purchase value.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Dutch government has imposed, on October 1st 2012, a tax on banks operating in the Netherlands. The base of this tax is bank liabilities, excluding BIS capital, guaranteed deposits and the liabilities of the insurance business (if any). The tariff distinguishes between short (0.044%) and long (0.022%) term liabilities. If the total tax base is lower than €20 billion, no tax will be imposed. Moreover, if the variable pay of at least one executive board member is more than 100% of the fixed salary, the total tax owed is multiplied by 1.1.

ING Bank, Rabobank and ABN AMRO face an O-SII of 2%, while SNS faces an O-SII buffer of 1%. At the same time, DNB announced an SRB of 3% for ING Bank, Rabobank and ABN AMRO. The higher of O-SII and SRB buffers applies so in  effect: ING Bank, Rabobank and ABN AMRO are subject to an additional capital requirement of 3% of risk-weighted assets, and SNS Bank of 1%. These buffers will be phased in between 2016 and 2019, with 2016 levels of 0.5% for ING Bank, Rabobank and ABN AMRO and 0.25% for SNS. The legal basis is the Dutch CRR/CRD IV Implementation Act.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: The Bank classifies receivables into the following categories: (i) regulary repaid: credit exposures for which repayment delay is up to one year at the time when the Treasury is becoming a debtor, consumer credit exposures for which repayment delay is up to 6 months, other credit exposures for which repayment delay is up to 1 month; (ii) under observation (this category is only for retail and other credit exposures) - regulary repaid loans that bank treats as more riskier under conditions defined by bank: retail credit exposures (excluding consumer loans) for which repayment delay is from 1 month up to 3 months, other credit exposures for which repayment delay is from 1 month up to 3 months; (iii) sub-standard (this category is only for retail and other credit exposures): retail credit exposures (excluding consumer loans) for which repayment delay is from 3 months up to 6 months, other credit exposures for which repayment delay is from 3 months up to 6 months; (iv) doubtful (consumer loans are excluded from this category) - repayment delay is between 6 months and 12 months or repayment delay is from 1 year to 2 years at the time when the Treasury is becoming a debtor; (v) lost: credit exposures for which repayment delay is above 2 years at the time when the Treasury is becoming a debtor, consumer credit exposures for which repayment delay is above 6 months, retail credit exposures (excluding consumer loans) for which repayment delay is above 12 months, other credit exposures for which repayment delay is above 12 months.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: Banks are required to hold specific provisions determined on an individual assessment of the risk inherent in receivables, but in an amount not less than: 1.5% for regulary repaid consumer credit, 1.5% for receivables and off-balance sheet items which are under observation. For non-performing loans and off-balance sheet items: 20% - for sub-standard receivables, 50% - for doubtful receivables, 100% - for lost receivables. The list of protections by which the specific provisions value can be reduced is more detailed.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
Banks may create general risk provision in order to cover unidentified banking risk.
Banks may recognize as cost any payment on a risk fund to cover any losses on loans. The maximum amount of such cost amounts to 1,5% of the average amount of outstanding loans and advances at the end of each quarter of the accounting year less specific provisions for lost receivables but not more than the payments for the general risk fund in that year.

Decree-Law No. 133/2009 of 2 June transposed into national legislation Directive 2008/48/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 April 2008 on credit agreements for consumers and repealing Council Directive 87/102/EEC. Article 28 of the Decree-Law establishes that Banco de Portugal should be responsible for identifying the relevant credit contracts and determining and publishing the maximum interest rates applicable on new credit consumer contracts, on a quarterly basis. Relevant consumer credit agreements for this purpose include personal loans, auto loans, credit cards and other consumer loans.
Maximum interest rates are determined as the average, increased by a quarter, of the annual effective percentage rate of charge (EAPR) charged by credit institutions in the previous quarter, for all the different types of contracts.

Accordingly, Deduction to own funds = Deposit amount x maturity x (Interest rate – Benchmark interest rate) x 0.01; where Interest rate: effective deposit interest rate, Benchmark interest rate: results from applying a spread over the benchmark market rate for the relevant period. - 50% of the market value of the property in question or 
- 60% of the mortgage lending value (in those Member States that have laid down rigorous criteria for the assessment of the mortgage lending value in statutory or regulatory provisions), whichever is lower. 

According to Basel III/CRR rules the value of the secured portion of exposure may not exceed 50% of the MV or 60% of the MLV of the property (there is no longer wording "whichever is lower"!).

Exemptions from the amortisation requirement will be allowed in certain situations, such as unemployment or sickness. description: Operational Risk was incorporated in the UK’s (FSA) handbook within Section 6 of the Prudential Sourcebook for Banks, Building Societies and Investment firms (BIPRU 6)  with effect from 01 January 2007  with the section relating the Advanced Measurement Approach being added with effect from 01.01 2008. BIPRU 6 is an ‘intelligent copy’ out from the Banking Consolidation Directive.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The total amount of a firm’s exposures to the same counterparty or group of connected clients may exceed 25% of the firm’s capital resources so long as the total amount of such exposures does not exceed €150 million. Where the amount of €150 million is higher than an amount equivalent to 25% of the firm’s capital resources, the firm must ensure the following: (i) the total amount of those exposures in relation to the same counterparty or group of connected clients does not exceed a reasonable limit in terms of the firm’s capital resources; and (ii) in any case, the limit in this rule must not exceed 100% of the firm’s capital resources.

category: Liquidity requirements and limits on currency and maturity mismatch
subcategory: Short-term liquidity coverage ratios incl. Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Under the FSA Policy Statement (09/16) on ‘Strengthening Liquidity Standards’, a subset of banks are required to hold a sufficient stock of high quality liquid assets (HQLA) to withstand two scenarios of stressed funding conditions (i.e. an acute bank specific funding shock lasting 14 days and less acute but more generalised deterioration in funding conditions lasting 3 months). Banks are subject to an Individual Liquidity Guidance (ILG) requirement, which is set by the supervisor on a firm-specific basis.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Revision of the phase-in of the bank levy. The rates for the calendar year 2011 will be: 01 March 2011 - 30 April 2011 - 0.1 per cent for short-term chargeable liabilities and 0.05 per cent for long-term chargeable equity and liabilities, 01 May 2011 - 31 December 2011 - 0.075 per cent for short-term chargeable liabilities and 0.0375 per cent for long-term chargeable equity and liabilities. Effectively this ensures that the rate applicable for 2011 would be 0.075 per cent for short-term chargeable liabilities and 0.0375 per cent for long-term chargeable equity and liabilities.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: An increase in the bank levy. Initially scheduled to reach 0.075 per cent from 2012 onwards. After the revision of the phase-in and an increase in the rate 0.078 perc rate for short-term chargeable liabilities effective from May 2011.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The bank levy intended to encourage banks to reduce the use of wholesale finance, with a view to reducing the risk of another financial crisis being triggered by liquidity issues.The rate for 2011 will be 0.05 per cent for short-term chargeable liabilities and 0.025 per cent for long-term chargeable equity and liabilities.It will rise to 0.075 per cent for short-term chargeable liabilities and 0.0375 per cent for long-term chargeable equity and liabilities in 2012.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Deactivation of an existing tool
description: With the introduction of the new BIPRU rules on large exposures, the 800% (of eligible capital) aggregate large exposure limit was abolished.

category: Limits on large exposures and concentration
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: With the introduction of the new BIPRU rules on large exposures, the 20% (of eligible capital) intragroup large exposure limit was abolished. Full exemption for exposures in the core UK group. Non-core large exposures group are subject o 100% limit. Non-trading book exposures are subject to a 100% limit (capital of core UK group). Trading book exposures to remaining connected counterparties subject to 500% limit. Non-trading book exposures subject to 25% limit.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 was amended by the Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act in 2013 to require UK banking groups with ‘core deposits’ (broadly those deposits from individuals and small businesses) to ring-fence their ‘core activities’ from risks in their group and broader financial markets. The legislation does this by restricting the activities such ‘ring-fenced banks’ can carry out, and requires the PRA to make certain rules in relation to ring-fencing.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: The bank levy is being raised from 0.078% to 0.088% from 1 January 2012.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: A recommendation in November 2011 by the UK Financial Policy Committee (FPC) that major UK firms disclose their leverage ratios using the Basel III definition as part of their regular reporting.

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: To ensure the Bank Levy raises at least £2½ billion each year, and takes account of the benefit to the banking sector from the additional reductions in corporation tax announced at Budget 2011, Budget 2012 and Autumn Statement 2012, the rate of the Bank Levy will increase to 0.130 per cent from 1 January 2013. A proportionate increase to 0.065 per cent will be made to the half rate, also with effect from 1 January 2013.

subcategory: Other capital requirements targeting most important institutions
action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The PRA should take steps to ensure that, by the end of 2013, major UK banks and building societies hold capital resources equivalent to at least 7% of their risk-weighted assets, as assessed on the basis described in Recommendation 13/Q1/1.(1) Relative to that benchmark, major UK banks and building societies in aggregate currently have a shortfall in capital of about £25 bn

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
A total capital ratio of 8% (CRR Art 92, 1(c)). 
Change on the scope of an existing tool: (i) CRR introduced some tightening to the definition of capital and RWA; (ii) CRR introduced loosening in areas, such as the preferential treatment of exposures to SME, less strict approach to exposures to some equity holdings, cancellation of deduction of expected loss surplus over provisions for banks using standardised approach etc.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Final fully-phased Tier 1 capital ratio of 6% (CRR Art 92, 1(b))

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by residential property
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Exposures fully and completely secured by mortgages on residential property 35%. Where required criteria are not met, a 100% risk weight applies. The part of the loan to which the 35 % risk weight is assigned does not exceed 80 % of the market value of the property in question or 80 % of the mortgage lending value of the property in question in those Member States that have laid down rigorous criteria for the assessment of the mortgage lending value in statutory or regulatory provisions.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) set out its intention to use the transitional provisions provided by the CRR to require firms to meet a Pillar 1 CET1 ratio of 4% of risk weighted assets from 1 January 2014 (rising to 4.5% from 1 January 2015)

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) set out its intention to use the transitional provisions provided by the CRR to require firms to meet a Pillar 1 Tier 1 ratio of 5.5% of risk weighted assets from 1 January 2014 (rising to 6% from 1 January 2015)

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Maintaining the existing level and scope of a tool
description: Exposures fully and completely secured by mortgages on commercial immovable property 50%. Where required criteria are not met, a 100% risk weight applies. Any part of an exposure that exceeds the mortgage value of the property shall be assigned the risk weight applicable to the unsecured exposures of the counterparty (Article 124(1) CRR). Immovable commercial property as collateral, up to the lower of the pledged amount and 50 % of the market value or 60 % of the mortgage lending value.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Final fully-phased Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5% (CRR Art 92, 1(a))

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Under Finance Act 2014, the bank levy rate had been increased to 0.156% for short term liabilities (and 0.078% for long terms equity and liabilities) from 1 January 2014.

action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: On 29 November 2013, the PRA issued a supervisory statement on capital and leverage ratios for major UK banks and building societies (SS3/13). The PRA set a 3% leverage ratio expectation for 8 major UK firms.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: The CCB rate set to 0%.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: Recommendation to limit the quarterly flow of new residential mortgages. New loans with LTI ratio at or above 4.5 cannot exceed 15% of the total number of the new mortgages.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description:
Interest rate stress tests to assess mortgage affordability
 Stress test whether borrowers could still afford the mortgage if the BoE rate increases by 3 percentage points over a 5 year period.

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: The PRA supervisory expectation SS3/13 was followed by a review of the leverage ratio by the FPC which was requested by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in November 2013 and concluded in October 2014. The FPC review established a strong case for introducing a UK leverage ratio framework ahead of an internationally agreed standard. The FPC asked the Government for power of Direction over to the PRA to implement its leverage ratio framework  comprising of a minimum 3% Tier 1 leverage ratio requirement and two buffers to address  systemic and countercyclical risks.  In April 2015, the Government gave the FPC new powers of Direction over the PRA in relation to leverage ratio tools.  On 1 July 2015, the FPC directed the PRA to implement a UK leverage ratio framework

subcategory: Risk weights on loans backed by commercial property
action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description:
Criteria for certain exposures secured by mortgages on commercial property. For purposes of Articles 124(2) and 126(2) of the CRR and in addition to the conditions set out therein, a firm may  treat exposures as fully and completely secured by mortgages on commercial immovable property located in the UK in accordance with Article 126 of the  CRR only where annual average losses stemming from lending secured by mortgages on commercial property located in the UK did not exceed 0.5% of risk-weighted exposure amounts over a representative period. A firm shall calculate the loss level referred to in this  rule on the basis of the aggregate market data for commercial property lending published by the PRA in accordance with Article 101(3) of the CRR. A firm may treat an exposure or any part of an exposure that is located in a jurisdiction that is not an EEA State as fully and completely secured for the purposes of Article 126 (1) of the CRR only if all of the following conditions are met: (i) annual average losses stemming from lending secured by mortgages on commercial property located in that jurisdiction did not exceed 0.5% of the exposure value over a representative period where: 
(a) there is sufficient evidence that the data used to determine the loss level referred to in this rule are of the same or better quality as the data required to be published under Article 101(3) of the CRR; and (b) it is reasonable to rely on such data; (2) the risk-weight that would be applied to that exposure or part of an exposure by the relevant supervisory authority in that jurisdiction is 50% or less. For the purposes of this rule 4.1 and 4.1A, a representative period shall be a time horizon of sufficient length and which includes a mix of good and bad years. [Note: Arts. 124(2) and 126(2) of the CRR]

category: Levy / Tax on financial institutions and activities
action_type: Change in the level of an existing tool
description: Further increases the rate of the bank levy to 0.21% for short term liabilities from 1 April 2015 (and 0.105% for long term equity and liabilities).

action_type: Change in the scope of an existing tool
description: In July 2015 the PRA consulted on implementing this framework for major UK PRA-regulated banks and building societies with consolidated retail deposits over £50bn from 1 January 2016 (see CP24/15). Subject to a review in 2017 of progress on international leverage ratio standards, the FPC expects to direct the PRA to extend the requirement to all banks, building societies and PRA-regulated investment firms from 2018. \Furthermore, the Bank of England's approach to stress testing the UK banking system, that informs a firm-specific capital buffer, uses a 3% leverage ratio threshold for firms subject to this exercise.

action_type: Activation of a new tool
description: On 15 December in accordance with Article 131 of the Capital Requirements Directive (2013/36/EU) (CRD), the PRA disclosed the 2015 list of UK headquartered Global Systemically Important Institutions (G-SIIs) and their respective sub-categories.  Applicable buffers are: HSBC Holdings Plc 2.5%, ​Barclays Plc 2%, The ​Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc ​1%, ​Standard Chartered Plc ​1%. These buffers will be applied and phased in from 1 January 2017 in line with Article 162(5) of the CRD. The list of G-SIIs and their sub-category allocations will be updated annually.
